timeline.description: Else Neuländer – Yva – becomes one of Weimar Berlin's most in-demand fashion and commercial photographers.
timeline.longDescription: During the Weimar Republic, many women rose to become well-known, successful photographers. Else Neuländer, born 1900, started out in the mid-1920s and soon became well established under the name Yva. Besides nude and portrait photography, her most lucrative commissions were for fashion and commercial photography; one specialty was photo-stories for the monthly magazine Uhu profiling the 'new' modern woman, with titles such as 'Lieschen Neumann wants to get ahead'. From 1930 to 1934 the Yva studio was located at Bleibtreu Strasse 17, on the corner of Mommsen Strasse. She took commissions from papers and magazines including Berliner Illustrierte Zeitung, Die Dame and Elegante Welt, and cooperated closely with her friend, doctor of art history Charlotte Weidler.

timeline.description: Nazi campaigns make Jewish photography careers nearly impossible, but the Schlüter Strasse studio keeps working – Helmut Newton trains under Yva.
timeline.longDescription: From 1933 the Yva studio was hit by Nazi campaigns and legislation: the newspaper Deutsche Nachrichten published a list of press photographers singling out Jews and foreigners, and after the establishment of the Reich Culture Chamber and the 'editors' law' it became virtually impossible for Jewish photographers to make a living. More and more of the newspapers Yva worked for were closed down, though the studio managed to keep publishing in the German press until 1936. In 1934 Else Neuländer married Alfred Hermann Simon, who looked after the financial side of the business, and they moved to Schlüter Strasse 45 – premises of 14 rooms whose roof garden, balconies and striking staircase featured often in the studio's photography. Yva employed about ten members of staff; Helmut Newton trained under her and later spoke of Yva's 'sacred halls'. As the situation worsened, her non-Jewish friend and associate Charlotte Weidler officially took over the studio, allowing Yva to continue working.

timeline.description: Forced to close by the order 'to eliminate Jews from the German economy', Yva performs forced labor as an X-ray assistant.
timeline.longDescription: In late 1938, Yva had to close down completely. In a testimonial for one of her employees she wrote that the business had to close because of the 'order to eliminate Jews from the German economy' of November 12, 1938. The couple moved several times in 1938 into ever smaller apartments; their last address was Bamberger Strasse 49, where they shared a furnished room. They had 34 cases put into storage at Hamburg harbor, suggesting they at one point considered emigration – but according to her friend Elisabeth Röttgers, Alfred Simon did not want to leave Berlin. After the onset of war, Yva performed forced labor as an X-ray assistant in the Jewish hospital; her husband as a street sweeper.

timeline.description: Yva and Alfred Simon are deported to Sobibór extermination camp. The date of their murder is not known.
timeline.longDescription: In early June 1942, the couple was arrested by the Gestapo and deported on June 13, 1942, to Sobibór extermination camp. The date of their murder is not known. In 1943 – one year later – transport companies and the head of the Berlin tax office began negotiations over the Simons' property, i.e. the 34 cases in storage in Hamburg: 13 were sold at auction and 21 were destroyed during a bombing raid.

timeline.description: Schlüter Strasse 45 has housed Hotel Bogota since 1965; commemorative brass stones for Yva and Alfred Simon were laid outside in 2005.
timeline.longDescription:
Yva's studio building at Schlüter Strasse 45 in Berlin-Charlottenburg survived the war and has housed Hotel Bogota since 1965. The hotel's proprietor, Joachim Rissmann, collects Yva's photography and pays tribute to her work and influence in an exhibition on the premises – the entrance hall with its striking staircase, the roof terrace and the doorways she used as backdrops for her fashion photography can still be recognized.

The site today

Two commemorative brass stones (Stolpersteine) were laid for Yva and her husband Alfred Simon outside the building in 2005.
